chapter.name: The Value of Work
chapter.blurb: Chapter 13 opens Theme E, 'Economic Life Around Us', by asking what different activities people engage in and what those activities contribute to everyday life. Through Anu and Kabir's neighbourhood -- Geeta Aunty the Air Force pilot, Kabir's retired-soldier grandfather now teaching Geography for free, and Anu's shopkeeper parents and software-engineer brother Rohan -- the chapter draws out a basic distinction: economic activities involve money or money's worth (a farmer selling produce, a lawyer's fee, a factory worker's pay), while non-economic activities do not generate income but matter because they are done out of gratitude, love, care and respect (a parent cooking for the family, a grandparent's free lesson). A second story, Kavya's visit to her aunt's village of Kamlapur, introduces the different forms economic activities can be paid in -- a technician's monthly salary, an aunt's salary plus a separate tutoring fee, and farm labourer Sahil's daily wage, part paid in mangoes as payment in kind -- before Rajesh the carpenter's worked example (wood bought for Rs 600, a chair sold for Rs 1,000) introduces value addition, the extra worth a maker's skill, time and effort adds to a raw material. The chapter then turns back to non-economic activities to show they are not lesser for generating no income: seva, or selfless service, seen in temples, gurudwaras, mosques and churches (such as a langar's free meals), and collective community participation through the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan and Van Mahotsav both show non-economic activity contributing to social welfare, personal wellbeing and quality of life.

scope_in.item: The distinction between economic activities (those that involve money or are performed in exchange for money or money's worth) and non-economic activities (those that do not generate income or wealth but are done out of feelings like gratitude, love, care and respect), introduced through the chapter's opening 'Big Questions' and the story of Anu, Kabir and their families; the chapter's list of economic activity examples -- a business person selling school bags in the market, a farmer selling produce in the market, a lawyer arguing a case and earning a fee, a truck driver transporting goods, and workers employed in a car manufacturing factory -- and the glossary terms Money's worth, Market and Fee

The chapter's non-economic activity examples -- parents cooking food for the family or helping their children with schoolwork, youth taking care of grandparents, and family members helping in the renovation of the house -- and the chapter's own contrast between paid and unpaid versions of similar activities, such as a school teacher's salaried teaching versus Kabir's grandfather's free Geography classes, Anu's mother's voluntary stitching group, and Rohan's unpaid weekend computer classes as against his salaried weekday software job; the glossary term Salary and its application to Geeta Aunty (an Air Force pilot) and Rohan

The 'Types of Economic Activities' section's forms of payment, told through Kavya's visit to Kamlapur: her uncle's monthly salary as a construction technician operating a bulldozer; her aunt's monthly salary at the village post office and separate weekly fee for evening online classes; and Sahil the farm labourer's daily wage, part-paid in cash and part in mangoes of equal value; the glossary terms Wage and Payment in kind

Value addition: the idea that economic activities add value at each stage of transforming something into another form, worked through Rajesh the carpenter's example -- buying wood for Rs 600 and selling a finished chair for Rs 1,000, with the remaining Rs 400 representing the monetary value of his own skill, time and effort

The 'Importance of Non-Economic Activities' section's introduction of seva (selfless service), seen in places such as temples, gurudwaras, mosques and churches, fostering satisfaction and gratitude and contributing to society without expecting anything in return; the example of langars, or community kitchens at gurudwaras, serving food to every visitor for free

Collective community participation as a form of non-economic activity, illustrated through the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan (the collective efforts of citizens, from individual homes to shared public places such as streets, roads and parks, to keep surroundings clean) and Van Mahotsav, the festival of forests that brings communities together for tree plantation drives to promote awareness of the value of trees and forest conservation; and the chapter's closing 'Before we move on' summary tying together economic activities, value addition, and non-economic activities' contribution to social welfare, personal wellbeing and quality of life

scope_out.item: The open-ended 'Let's Explore' and 'Think About It' prompts throughout the chapter (e.g. filling in the blank activity table for Anu's and Kabir's story, listing two new money-related value-creation examples, identifying local community practices and festivals, and reflecting on personal non-economic activities) and the closing 'Questions, activities and projects' (e.g. illustrating types of economic activities with examples, commenting on the value of community service)
scope_out.reason: These are discussion, activity or project prompts without one single fixed correct answer; where a prompt points to a specific stated fact (such as the definitions or the Rajesh value-addition figures), that fact is tested directly instead of the open-ended question around it

scope_out.item: Specific rupee amounts for anyone's salary, wage or fee other than Rajesh's wood-and-chair figures on page 190 (Rs 600 for wood, Rs 1,000 for the chair) -- no numeric figure is given anywhere in the chapter for Geeta Aunty's, Rohan's, Kavya's uncle's, Kavya's aunt's or Sahil's actual pay
scope_out.reason: Inventing numbers the book itself does not give would test a fact that does not exist in this source; only Rajesh's carpentry example carries real figures to calculate with

scope_out.item: Formal economics vocabulary such as GDP, national income, the primary/secondary/tertiary sector classification, employment/unemployment statistics, inflation, saving, banking, loans, or minimum wage law
scope_out.reason: None of this is named anywhere in the chapter; it explains economic and non-economic activity only through everyday examples and payment terms (salary, wage, fee, payment in kind, value addition), not through macroeconomic concepts a general economics syllabus might otherwise supply

scope_out.item: Which specific religion is associated with a temple, gurudwara, mosque or church, or any detail about the named places in the photo captions (the Golden Temple, or any particular temple distributing prasad) beyond their use as examples of where seva happens
scope_out.reason: The chapter lists the four places together only as settings where seva can be seen, without explaining or testing which faith each building belongs to, or giving any further detail about the specific places pictured

scope_out.item: The 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, labour rights or laws, trade unions, or any other legal/constitutional basis for how wages, salaries or working conditions are regulated
scope_out.reason: The chapter describes salary, wage, fee and payment in kind only as everyday payment terms illustrated through its characters' stories, never through labour law or constitutional provisions

scope_out.item: The 'Noodles' page label at the end of the chapter
scope_out.reason: It is only the book's running joke name ('Notes and Doodles') for a blank creative-notes page and carries no factual content of its own

concepts.name: Economic activities: definition, examples and key terms
concepts.description: What counts as an economic activity, the chapter's example set, and the glossary terms Money's worth, Market, Fee and Salary.
concepts.idea: Economic activities are activities that involve money, or are performed in exchange for money or money's worth, for the people involved.
concepts.rule: An activity is economic if payment changes hands in some form -- a sale in a market, a fee for a professional service, or a salary from an employer -- regardless of what the activity itself is.
concepts.example: A lawyer arguing a case and earning a fee, and Geeta Aunty, an Air Force pilot who receives a salary, are both performing economic activities.

concepts.name: Value addition in economic activities
